passage:
Sunday night
Convocation photos went up. Everyone's captions have a city in them: Berlin, Bengaluru, "back to Guwahati." I have twelve browser tabs open: a job in Pune, a fellowship in Odisha, a master's in Canada, my uncle's offer at the factory. Every one of them looks right for about ten minutes. Mummy says her son can't choose a shirt, let alone a city.
Wasim called. He's joining his dad's clinic, done, decided. Part of me envied him. Part of me thought, but you'll never know what else you could have been.
It's amazing that I can go anywhere. It's also terrifying. What if I pick the wrong door and the good one closes?
Wasim said, "Pick two, give them a month each, close the rest." Closing tabs now. Hands a bit shaky.
Suraj

qa.q: How many browser tabs did Suraj have open?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Suraj have when Wasim said he had decided?
qa.a: He envied Wasim's certainty but also felt Wasim would never know what else he could have been.

qa.q: Why is Wasim's advice to pick two and give each a month useful?
qa.a: It shrinks the choice to something manageable and tests options for real, instead of freezing over twelve.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel about his own settled choice?
qa.a: He may feel relieved not to face so many doors, though he might sometimes wonder about paths he didn't try.

grounding: A graduate facing many careers and cities feels both excited and frozen, and a friend helps him narrow the choice.

passage: The evening bus from the district college dropped Vaibhav at the crossroads of his small town, his degree rolled up in a plastic tube. At home his sister Indu was sorting apricots on the verandah. "So, graduate sahib, what now?" she teased. He sat beside her. "That's the problem, didi. A company interview in Delhi. Teaching at the block school. Coaching for the government exam. Or staying to help Papa with the orchard." He rolled an apricot in his palm. "Every one looks good until I think about the others. Then I feel sick that I'll lose them." Indu handed him the sorting basket. "You can't eat all the apricots at once. Try one properly." He laughed, but that night he wrote the four options on a page and crossed one out.

qa.q: What was Indu sorting on the verandah?
qa.a: Apricots.

qa.q: What is Vaibhav afraid of when he says he feels sick?
qa.a: He fears that choosing one path means losing all the others, so the many options feel heavy as well as exciting.

qa.q: What small step did Vaibhav take that night, and why does it help?
qa.a: He wrote the four options down and crossed one out, making the choice smaller and easier to face.

qa.q: How does Indu see her brother's dilemma?
qa.a: She treats it lightly but kindly, teasing him and reminding him he can't try everything at once.

grounding: A new graduate back in his small town sees many possible paths and feels both excited and afraid of choosing wrongly.

passage:
Two weeks after graduation, Siddiq sat on the steps outside Thabo's flat in Johannesburg, a laptop balanced on his knees. Four tabs: a mining firm in Rustenburg, a teaching fellowship in Durban, a master's offer in Lisbon, and his aunt's shop in Cape Town.
"Look at this," he said. "Any of them could be my whole life. That's amazing, right?"
"So why do you look sick?"
"Because any of them could be the wrong whole life." He opened a fifth tab: a classmate's post from London, new job, new city, new partner. "And everyone else seems sure."
Thabo closed the laptop gently. "You've been comparing for three hours. Which one did you think about in the shower this morning?"
Siddiq was quiet. "Durban."
"Then start there. You can change later."
Siddiq laughed, shakily. It felt thrilling and terrifying at once.

qa.q: How many tabs did Siddiq have open at first?
qa.a: He had four tabs open.

qa.q: Why does Siddiq look sick even though he calls his options amazing?
qa.a: He is excited by the possibilities but dreads choosing the wrong life, especially while comparing himself with a classmate who seems sure.

qa.q: What turning point did Thabo offer, and why might it help?
qa.a: Thabo closed the laptop and asked which option Siddiq thought of in the shower, cutting through endless comparison to a first step.

qa.q: How might Thabo see Siddiq's three hours of comparing?
qa.a: Thabo seems to see it as a trap that feeds dread rather than helping, which is why the laptop gets closed.

grounding: A new graduate faces many careers and cities with both excitement and dread, caught in comparison until a friend helps him pick a first step.

passage:
The career fair filled the university sports hall with sixty stalls and a noise like a railway station. Akash, twenty-one, had a bag of brochures by eleven: a bank in Mumbai, a solar startup in Pune, a rural fellowship in Odisha, a master's in Germany.
Jahnavi found him on the bleachers. "You look like you've seen a ghost."
"I've seen sixty futures." He laughed, then didn't. "It's exciting. Every stall is a different me. But if I pick solar and the bank was right, I'll spend ten years comparing."
"You already are. You've read the bank brochure four times."
"Because Vivek got the bank, and he posts about it every day."
"Vivek is not you. Circle two you'd be curious to wake up to. Just two."
Akash took out a pen. His hand hovered, then circled solar and Odisha.

qa.q: How many stalls filled the sports hall?
qa.a: Sixty stalls filled the sports hall.

qa.q: What does Akash mean by 'Every stall is a different me'?
qa.a: He feels excited by all the possible selves but also dreads choosing wrongly and comparing forever.

qa.q: What small step did Jahnavi suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Circling just two options he'd be curious to wake up to, which narrows the choice so it doesn't freeze him.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Akash's rereading of the bank brochure?
qa.a: Jahnavi sees it as comparison with Vivek rather than real interest, which is why Jahnavi reminds him that Vivek is not him.

grounding: A graduate at a career fair feels both excitement and dread at many possible futures, stuck comparing until a friend helps narrow the choice.

passage: Tomas had graduated in June and by September he'd opened seventeen browser tabs. A design job in Porto. A master's in Berlin. His aunt's café in Lisbon. A volunteer year in Peru. Emil, his flatmate, was going to Copenhagen and seemed sure of it. Each morning Tomas woke up excited, and each night he couldn't sleep, sure that whatever he picked would be the wrong one, and he'd see someone on his feed living the life he'd rejected. He hadn't applied to anything. "You know," Emil said one evening, passing him a beer, "you're not choosing forever. You're choosing next." Tomas stared at the tabs. Then he closed twelve of them. The other five he wrote on a paper, and ranked by the one that made his stomach flip in a good way.

qa.q: How many browser tabs had Tomas opened by September?
qa.a: Tomas had opened seventeen browser tabs.

qa.q: What was Tomas feeling each night?
qa.a: Tomas felt anxious and full of dread, sure he'd choose wrongly and see someone living the life he'd turned down.

qa.q: What small step helped Tomas get unstuck, and why?
qa.a: Closing twelve tabs and ranking the rest on paper narrowed endless options into a choice he could actually make.

qa.q: How might Emil see Tomas's situation?
qa.a: Emil, already sure of his own path, seems to see Tomas as overwhelmed and wants to help by reminding him he's choosing next, not forever.

grounding: A graduate faced with many careers and cities feels excitement and dread, and the open choices freeze him until he narrows them.

passage: The placement cell at the university smelled of printer ink. Bhavna had three offers on the table: a start-up in Bengaluru, a government research post in Delhi, and a scholarship to study in Scotland. Every friend had an opinion. Every cousin had posted a success story. Pradeep sir, the placement officer, noticed she'd filled in the acceptance form and crossed it out four times. "Bhavna, what's happening?" She laughed shakily. "Sir, I'm so lucky. And I feel like I'm going to throw up. If I pick wrong, I've wasted all of it." Pradeep sir slid a blank paper across. "Write what you'd want your normal Tuesday to look like in two years. Not the title. The Tuesday." She stared at it. Slowly she wrote: a lab, a small team, quiet mornings. It narrowed the choice at once.

qa.q: How many times did Bhavna cross out the acceptance form?
qa.a: Bhavna crossed it out four times.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she said she might throw up?
qa.a: Bhavna felt both lucky and full of dread, afraid of wasting her chances by picking wrong.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep sir's "normal Tuesday" exercise help?
qa.a: It moved Bhavna from comparing titles to picturing daily life, which quickly narrowed the choice.

qa.q: How might Pradeep sir see Bhavna's struggle?
qa.a: Pradeep sir seems to see a capable student frozen by too many options, and wants to help her find her own answer rather than give one.

grounding: A graduate with several offers feels both lucky and terrified of choosing wrong, and a concrete exercise helps unfreeze the choice.

passage:
Dear Pema,
Thank you for your postcard from Thimphu. I've stuck it above my desk, next to the list of everything I could do now that I've graduated.
The list is the problem. I could take the Mumbai job. Or the fellowship in rural Rajasthan. Or stay in Hyderabad near Ammi. Or do nothing for six months and write. Every option is a door and I'm standing in the corridor. Some mornings it's thrilling. Most nights I scroll through classmates' updates and feel sick, like I'm the only one who hasn't chosen.
You once told me in Bhutan that you pick one road and walk it long enough to know it. I think that's what I'm scared of: not choosing wrong, but never finding out because I keep comparing.
So I've set a date. By the first of next month, I'll pick one door.
Much love,
Ayesha

qa.q: Where did Pema's postcard come from?
qa.a: Pema's postcard came from Thimphu.

qa.q: What does Ayesha feel most nights when scrolling classmates' updates?
qa.a: Ayesha feels sick and anxious, as if everyone else has chosen and Ayesha is the only one left behind.

qa.q: Why is setting a date a sensible step for Ayesha?
qa.a: A deadline limits endless comparing, so Ayesha can walk one road long enough to learn from it.

qa.q: How might Pema feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Pema might feel moved that the advice from Bhutan stayed with Ayesha, and want to encourage the first step.

grounding: A graduate sees many possible paths and feels both thrill and dread, with endless comparison freezing the choice until a deadline is set.

passage:
"You asked how graduation feels. I'm Uday, twenty-two. Honestly, it's like standing in a huge sweet shop with no idea what to pick.
I could take the job in Bengaluru, or do a master's in Delhi, or join my friend Vaibhav's startup in Pune, or take a year off to travel. Every option looks good. Every option could be a mistake.
Some mornings I'm so excited I can't sit still. Other nights I lie awake scrolling my classmates' posts, comparing. Someone's in Germany. Someone got into a top firm. Everyone seems sure.
Vaibhav says, 'Just pick one and try. You can change later.'
Maybe. But I keep thinking, what if I pick wrong and waste years? So I haven't picked anything yet."

qa.q: Where is Vaibhav's startup?
qa.a: It's in Pune.

qa.q: How does Uday feel about all the options?
qa.a: Uday feels both excited and afraid of choosing wrongly, and anxious when comparing with classmates.

qa.q: What could help Uday move past being frozen?
qa.a: Take Vaibhav's advice to try one option, knowing it can be changed later, and limit comparison scrolling.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see Uday's dilemma?
qa.a: Vaibhav thinks Uday should just pick one and try, since choices can be changed later.

grounding: A graduate sees many possible paths and feels both excitement and dread of choosing wrongly, frozen and comparing.

passage:
May: Arohi graduated from college in Chandigarh with four options: a bank job, a design course, her aunt's business, or a gap year. She felt thrilled.
July: She still hadn't decided. She spent nights comparing herself to classmates' posts: one in London, one at a big firm. Her friend Vinita asked, "Which one feels right?" Arohi burst into tears. "All of them. None of them. What if I ruin my life?"
September: Vinita helped her list what mattered most: creativity, staying near family, learning. The design course in the city fitted best. Arohi signed up, still a little scared. "It's not forever," Vinita said. Arohi nodded, feeling lighter.

qa.q: How many options did Arohi have after graduating?
qa.a: She had four options.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when she burst into tears in July?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and afraid, frozen by the fear of ruining her life with the wrong choice.

qa.q: How did Vinita help Arohi move forward?
qa.a: She helped her list what mattered most, which pointed to the design course, and reminded her it's not forever.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel when Arohi finally signs up?
qa.a: Vinita likely feels relieved and happy to see her friend unstuck.

grounding: Over months, a graduate with many options feels both excitement and dread, freezes and compares, then chooses with help.

passage:
"Jatin, you think you have too many choices? Let your old Chacha tell you.
When I was twenty-two, I, Yusuf, finished my degree in Aligarh. My uncle offered a job in his Mumbai shop. A professor offered research. A friend wanted me in his printing press. I could have gone to the Gulf for good money.
I was excited for a week. Then I froze. For three months I did nothing, just compared myself to friends who seemed sure.
My mother finally said, 'Pick the one you'd regret not trying. You can always change.'
I chose research. Later I left it and joined the press anyway! But choosing got me moving.
Having many doors is a gift, beta. Just don't stand in the corridor forever."

qa.q: How long did Yusuf do nothing after freezing?
qa.a: For three months.

qa.q: How did young Yusuf feel during those three months?
qa.a: He felt stuck and anxious, comparing himself to friends who seemed sure, after a week of excitement.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: His mother told him to pick the one he'd regret not trying, which got him moving into research.

qa.q: How might Yusuf's mother have felt watching him do nothing for three months?
qa.a: She was probably worried and wanted to help him move forward.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a graduate, feeling excited then frozen by many choices, and moving only after picking one to try.

passage: Yamini had until midnight to accept one of three offers: a design job in Bengaluru, a fellowship teaching in rural Odisha, or a master's seat in Pune. At nine her laptop charger died, and the corner cafe was closing at ten. She sat at the last table with her phone at twelve per cent, three tabs open, heart racing. Each one looked like a different life. Each one meant losing the other two. She texted Yusuf: 'what if i pick wrong and regret it forever.' He replied: 'what if all three are good and you're just choosing a flavour.' Yamini laughed, then stopped comparing salaries and asked herself one question: which one did she want to wake up to next Monday? At 9:52, with four per cent left, she accepted the fellowship, and felt terrified and light at once.

qa.q: What were Yamini's three offers?
qa.a: A design job in Bengaluru, a fellowship teaching in rural Odisha, and a master's seat in Pune.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling at the cafe table?
qa.a: Yamini felt excited but anxious, heart racing, afraid of picking wrong and regretting it forever.

qa.q: What question helped Yamini break the freeze?
qa.a: Which one she wanted to wake up to next Monday, which cut through endless comparison of salaries.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see Yamini's dilemma?
qa.a: Yusuf sees it lightly, as choosing between three good flavours rather than risking a wrong life.

grounding: Under a deadline a graduate with three open futures feels thrill and dread and breaks the freeze with one simple question.

passage: Every night in her Mumbai hostel room, Nirmala did the same thing: opened her college batch's photos and compared. Priyanka at a startup in Berlin. Faisal doing a PhD in Chennai. Someone engaged, someone backpacking. Nirmala had graduated in May and still hadn't applied anywhere. Every door looked open, and that was the problem. If she chose one, the others would close, and what if she chose the dull one? Her brother Suraj came to visit on Sunday and found her with twelve job tabs open and none filled in. 'You're shopping, not choosing,' he said, closing the laptop. 'Pick two. Apply. You can change later.' Nirmala felt a flash of annoyance, then relief. That night she applied to two jobs and stopped looking at the batch photos.

qa.q: How many job tabs did Nirmala have open?
qa.a: Twelve job tabs, none filled in.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling while comparing her batch's photos?
qa.a: Nirmala felt restless and anxious, excited by open doors but dreading choosing the dull one.

qa.q: Why was Suraj's advice to pick two a helpful one?
qa.a: It broke the freeze by making the choice small and reversible, stopping the endless comparison.

qa.q: How might Suraj see his sister's situation?
qa.a: Suraj sees her as stuck shopping rather than choosing, and wants to help her move.

grounding: A graduate facing endless options freezes and compares herself with others until her brother nudges her to choose.

passage:
'So Nikhil's moving to Delhi and wants me to come,' Rekha said, lying on Swati's bed.
'And?'
'And Kochi has that museum job. And my cousin says Bengaluru is where everything happens. And I'm twenty-two. What if I choose a city because of a boy and it's the wrong boy? What if I stay and miss the right one?'
'You're doing the thing again.'
'What thing?'
'Imagining ten futures and living in none.' Swati sat up. 'Which one makes you excited, not just not-scared?'
Rekha was quiet a long time. 'The museum. Honestly. And Nikhil... I'd visit.'
'Then that's a start.'
'But what if—'
'Rekha. Every choice closes doors. That's what makes it a choice.'
Rekha pulled the pillow over her face and laughed into it. 'I hate that you're right.'

qa.q: Where is Nikhil moving?
qa.a: To Delhi.

qa.q: What is Rekha feeling as she lists the options?
qa.a: Rekha feels excited by the options but anxious and frozen, afraid of choosing the wrong city or the wrong person.

qa.q: What question from Swati helps, and why?
qa.a: 'Which one makes you excited, not just not-scared?' It shifts Rekha from avoiding regret to noticing what she actually wants.

qa.q: How does Swati see Rekha's habit?
qa.a: Swati sees it as imagining ten futures and living in none, and gently pushes Rekha to accept that choosing means closing doors.

grounding: A young graduate weighing cities, jobs and a partner feels excitement and dread until a friend helps her notice what she wants.

passage: The Puja holidays after graduation were the strangest two weeks I've had. Everyone at the pandal asked the same thing: "So, what next?" And I had too many answers. A job offer in Pune. A master's form half filled for Delhi. Thomas's idea that we both apply to a design fellowship in Bengaluru. Even my aunt's hint about a match from Salt Lake. Each night I opened all the tabs and compared salary, city, what my classmates were posting. Each night I closed them without deciding. It felt like standing in a sweet shop with every tray open and my stomach in knots. On Dashami, Thomas said, "You don't have to pick your whole life, Bidisha. Just the next year." That line got me to sign the Pune offer. I still wonder about the others.

qa.q: Where was the job offer?
qa.a: In Pune.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel while comparing all the options each night?
qa.a: Bidisha felt excited but anxious, with a stomach in knots, afraid of choosing wrongly and so closing every tab without deciding.

qa.q: What made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Thomas's reminder to pick just the next year made the choice small enough to face, which broke the freeze.

qa.q: What might Thomas have noticed during the holidays?
qa.a: Thomas probably saw Bidisha stuck in endless comparison, which is why the advice shrank the question to a single year.

grounding: A graduate facing many careers, cities and even a match feels both excitement and dread, and freezes until the choice is made smaller.
